Anne Vallayer-Coster was one of four women admitted to the royal academy before the Revolution, elected at twenty-six, and her Portrait of a violinist carries that certification: maker named, date fixed, reputation attached. Here it went the other way. David's studio taught women in a room of their own and in a shared idiom of bare grounds and cool light, and the idiom outlived the record, sitter renamed then unnamed, author narrowed to a circle that still formally includes the master. What an academy wrote down has outlasted what it merely taught.

replacedBy.beside: The same white muslin, gathered high under the bust and filmed with gauze where skin shows pink through it, had crossed the Channel four years later, when Lawrence painted Lady Mary Templetown and Her Eldest Son, also in the National Gallery of Art. Both women wear a dark band bound through the hair, and both pictures spend their one saturated red beside the white: a crimson shawl here, coral beads there. What the gown says has changed. Against this bare grey ground and plain wooden chair it is the argument itself, republican plainness unsoftened. In an English autumn wood, a small heir leaning on her knee, it has become the costume of a devoted mother.

beside: Another painter bent his whole attention onto a tangled mass of roots at close range, and the rhyme between them is not idle. Tree Roots has been matched to a specific slope a hundred and fifty metres from the inn where Van Gogh lodged, and the argument runs that he made it on the last day he worked. Sargent's grip on limestone comes out of the opposite condition: the first free autumn after he shut down a portrait practice, this ground chosen precisely because nobody had asked for it. A few square yards of hillside turn out to be enough ground for a career to end on, or restart on.

replacedBy.beside: Follow the roots down to where wood meets stone: that seam is the picture, and nothing above it may compete. Ruisdael's Forest Scene, two and a half centuries older and also in Washington, puts the same seam at its right edge, where a birch snapped off in raw orange stumps still clamps its roots over a lichened rock while its trunk falls towards a stream. Ruisdael surrounds his grip with a sky of piled cloud, a waterfall and a couple on a path, and turns it into a lesson in decay. Sargent crops away the sky and the crown, and a grip that is simply holding has to carry the whole canvas.

beside: Set this beside a picture where the unfinishing is not staged but real. The Needlewoman shows a woman at her sewing with the hands stopped at pale hooks, and Velázquez never let the canvas out of his own lodgings; it was still there in the inventory taken at his death. Carracci puts incompleteness at the centre of his subject and then resolves every inch of it — the body under construction is itself fully made, brought to a finish the goddess herself has not reached. One painter dramatises the moment before completion. The other simply stops working, and lets the stopping stand as the picture.

replacedBy.beside: Venus with a Mirror, also in Washington and some thirty-five years older, gives a goddess the same staff and the same chores: a child at the right braces the glass while a second lifts a wreath over her head. By the time Titian lets us in, though, the work is done. Pearls are set in her braids, bracelets circle both arms, rings sit on her fingers, and the mirror is tilted to hand us a second, softer Venus. Carracci opens the door earlier. Hair is still being parted and bound, a child is still lifting pearls out of the casket, another works at her foot, and the glass his child hoists is near-black, giving back almost nothing yet.

beside: The other hand in this room belongs to Manet, and he does not always arrive that way. Four summers later, painting across the river from Monet, he made Bords de Seine à Argenteuil by taking on the younger man's swift broken touch for the water while keeping his own thick paint and rich blacks — borrowing, chosen, inside his own canvas, with nothing at stake but a summer. Here the traffic runs the other way and on a deadline: he picks up someone else's brushes, on someone else's picture, hours before it must go out, and the mother's face and black dress come back in his shorthand. Same generosity, opposite cost.

replacedBy.beside: Two women side by side, one in white with a blue ribbon in her hair, and a page that claims attention: all of it returns twenty-three years later in Girls at the Piano, in Paris's Musée d'Orsay. There the page claims both of them. The blonde plays from the score and grips its corner, the dark-haired girl leans over her shoulder with an elbow on the music, heads nearly touching. Here the book belongs to one woman only. The mother bends into it, both hands on the boards; the daughter in white sits upright beside her, hands slack in her lap, attending to nothing but the painter. Renoir paints attention shared; Morisot, one room holding two separate conditions.

beside: The same ambition that arranges this family into one calm interlocking mass drives Watson and the Shark, painted a year later as Copley's other bid for London. Here he proves he belongs by cohesion: eight sitters pressed still, a household shown surviving the ocean crossing intact. There he proves it by rupture, a boy naked in the water and a crew lunging as jaws break the surface. One canvas stakes the newcomer's arrival on tenderness holding under strain, the other on terror seized at its peak, yet both are the provincial announcing he can command a large multi-figure stage. The domestic embrace and the harbor emergency are the same wager run at opposite temperatures.

replacedBy.beside: A family pressed into one arc fills this canvas, and through an opening at the upper right a green valley runs to blue hills, one small house on a slope, nobody in it. Benjamin West's Colonel Guy Johnson and Karonghyontye, painted in London the same year, 1776, and likewise in Washington's National Gallery of Art, sets a family against its country in a small gap at the lower left: a waterfall, a bark shelter, a mother holding an infant, men at a fire. West gives his foreground to an officer and the Mohawk leader, and leaves that family at home in its land. Copley's family holds the foreground, and nothing in its valley says which country it is.

beside: The same fantasy geology, the same bargain of faith felt as scale, turns up in The Penitence of Saint Jerome — but there it is the master's own hand rather than a borrowed formula. Set the two side by side and the invention is identical: eroded pinnacles reared like broken teeth, a lone devotional figure shrunk to a thread crossing an enormous world. What differs is the stakes of authorship. One picture originates the device and signs for it; the other repeats it so convincingly that it kept imperial company for generations before scholarship caught the copyist. The world-landscape is the same wager made twice, once at its source and once in faithful echo.

replacedBy.beside: The donkey's road runs between two kinds of country: pale splintered rock towering over it, and to the right a valley falling away to the horizon with a white walled town in its greens. Less than a century later Rembrandt stopped the same journey for the night in Nocturnal Landscape with the Holy Family resting on the flight into Egypt, now in Ireland's National Gallery. A small fire under a tree lights the seated family and some cattle; on the hill above, a dark castle shows a few lit windows. The anonymous follower of Patinir who painted this panel lays the whole world out by daylight. Rembrandt's night takes it away, and refuge shrinks to the reach of one fire.

beside: Boldini made the same bargain again on a canvas nearly thirty times the area, elsewhere in this collection. La Marquise Luisa Casati avec des plumes de paon, in the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea in Rome, was begun twenty-two years after this panel: a hundred and thirty-six by a hundred and eighty-six centimetres, peacock plumes arching back over the sitter's shoulder, the ground around her churned into olive and black. In both, one head is held still while everything around it is weather. There the wager is placed at showpiece scale, on a canvas he reworked for years and kept; here it is placed on a panel a hand can cover, on a woman nobody named.

replacedBy.beside: Head lowered, eyes on her own hands, a woman busy at a chore with no thought of looking up: The Milkmaid, at the Rijksmuseum, is the touchstone for a moment nobody performs, painted more than two centuries before this panel. Vermeer spreads his attention evenly across the room. The bread crust gets raised dots of paint, the bare wall behind her keeps its nails and nail holes, and the plaster is watched as hard as her face. Boldini rations. One head is modelled to the lash, the bather's lowered eye and the gold at her throat; the wall beside it, the floor, the bird and the second woman are taken at the speed of a decision.

beside: The room this picture documents has a descendant in this collection. Sixty-six years after these tailcoats filed past the flower pieces, Warsaw's art public — the very institution this canvas shows being born in a borrowed university hall — mobbed a single painting at the Zachęta: Podkowiński's Szał uniesień, which its own maker attacked with a knife thirty-six days into the show. The two works bracket the same story from either end: here, looking at pictures is still a decorous novelty being learned; there, it has become a public passion strong enough to destroy what it looks at. This canvas stayed in Warsaw; Szał, restored, hangs in the Sukiennice in Kraków.

replacedBy.beside: A room built for looking, and the one person in it who has stopped: that is the whole of New York Movie, at the Museum of Modern Art, painted in 1939. The show there is a sliver of grey screen at the far left, the audience a scatter of dark heads, and the light goes to an usherette leaning in a lit alcove, hand at her chin, eyes down, her mind elsewhere. Kasprzycki weights it the other way. His show fills a wall, his audience stands in daylight, and looking is graded posture by posture, from a man folded double at a low landscape to men by the windows, backs to the art, several turning to look at you.

beside: Zorn hangs elsewhere in this collection, and the two portraits are the same wager placed at opposite stakes. Six years after this, Mrs. Walter Rathbone Bacon, now at the Metropolitan Museum, took the handful-of-strokes manner to the American market at showpiece scale — a seated grandee on a very tall canvas, her collie against her side, a likeness as public performance where this one stays close, a picture the sitter kept in the family for thirty-six years. There the wager is placed in public, at full scale; here it is placed close and small — and the strokes are exactly as few.

replacedBy.beside: A still head beside a storm of loaded paint is also the plan of Blumen und Tochter Wilhelmine, painted by Lovis Corinth twenty-nine years later and held by the Kunstmuseum Basel: his daughter at the right, eyes lowered under a pink bow, a heaped bouquet of lilac and white churning across the left. The bargain struck here is refused there. Zorn spends nearly all his finish on one face that meets you and lets everything behind it come apart, so the gold bird at full wingspan reads as weather round a fixed point. Corinth gives the child the same gouged strokes as the flowers, a dark smear for each eye, and her stillness holds with no finish to protect it.

beside: The version he made outdoors is in this collection too. Wheat Field with Cypresses hangs at the Metropolitan Museum — the same pair of cypresses on the right, the same olive scrub, the same high crest of wheat, on a canvas all but the same size — painted in the field in early summer 1889 and counted by him among the best work of that season. This one is the September repetition, worked up in the studio from a drawing. There the field was in front of him; here it was not, and every curl of that sky is a decision taken a second time.

replacedBy.beside: Weigh the cypress against the wheat: a dark spire climbing almost to the top edge over grain that is ripe and still uncut. The Harvesters, painted by Bruegel more than three centuries earlier and now in New York's Metropolitan Museum, builds its field on the same hinge, a single tree rising out of ripe wheat with open country beyond. Under Bruegel's pear the cutting is half done, sheaves stand in cones, and the reapers eat in its shade while one sleeps flat on his back. The year turns there through work and a meal. Nobody walks in Van Gogh's field, no scythe has reached it, and the turning is left to the tree, a mourner rooted beside the ripeness.

beside: Monet painted its companion from sea level, and both canvases are now at the Metropolitan. Regatta at Sainte-Adresse comes out of the same summer of 1867 on the same stretch of Normandy coast — cooler and breezier, though just as sunlit — and it gives the Channel the audience this one withholds: a knot of holidaymakers on the shingle, facing out, the racing sails strung across the middle distance in front of them. The same water, painted from the beach rather than the wall above it, with the crowd turned toward it.

replacedBy.beside: Eugène Manet on Isle of Wight, Berthe Morisot's picture at the Musée Marmottan Monet, painted eight years after this terrace, seats a man in a straw hat in profile, red flowers between him and a harbour of masts, two figures at a rail beyond. Both set a comfortable household at ease above a harbour full of boats. Monet puts his father in full sun among blazing gladioli, counting every sail and smoke-trail in the Channel. Morisot keeps her husband indoors behind a sash window, paints the pots on the sill more firmly than anything outside, and lets the harbour go in a few scratches. Both men sit idle for a painter in the family; Morisot's painter is his wife.

beside: Twenty-three years after this, Renoir built an entire picture around a page of marks that read as music. In Girls at the Piano, at the Musée d'Orsay, hair, dress and curtain are laid in with a feathering like this one — though the faces are blended smoother and the gilt fittings drawn in firm line — but every diagonal in the room, the leaning arm, the curtain, the music stand, converges on the open score, which he keeps the brightest and coolest white on the canvas. Here the readable thing is lettering, a commercial notice on a café flank, off to one side; there the page is what the painting is for.

replacedBy.beside: Leisure on the Seine, swimmers and sails, comes round again in Bathers at Asnières, at the National Gallery, London, fifteen years on, and Seurat holds still everything Renoir lets move. His bank is open grass, not a café raft, and his people keep apart: a youth in red trunks sits at the water's edge staring out, a man lies flat under a bowler, a boy waist-deep in a red cap cups his hands to call, while factory chimneys smoke across the river. Each figure is sealed inside its own outline. Here the crowd presses together on the pontoon, top hats and pale dresses running into one another, and the afternoon is a murmur rather than a pose.

beside: The far end of this bargain hangs in the same building, the National Gallery in London. Samson and Delilah, painted twenty-seven years earlier, is also on oak and also built around an act caught before it finishes — but it is night, indoors, and everything is crushed into one candlelit huddle, a barber's blade closing on a sleeping man's hair while soldiers wait in the doorway. That one was made for a patron's house; this one Rubens made for himself, on ground he had just bought and still owned at his death. Here the deed the picture waits on is a gun levelled at partridges from a ditch, small, in a bottom corner; there it is dead centre, and it ends a man.

replacedBy.beside: A house tucked under dark trees at the left, a farm cart, a dog in front and tiny workers in bright fields to the right: The Hay Wain, painted by Constable nearly two centuries later and housed with it at the National Gallery, follows this plan. Both show a working valley from its own ground, held on opposite terms. Rubens bought his late, and paints a holding at work at dawn: the cart loaded and leaving the frame, cows being milked, a man with a gun waiting on partridges. Constable's was his by birth, and nothing in it answers to him. The cottage is Willy Lott's, the cart stands empty in the ford, and the weather does the moving.

beside: Its companion elsewhere in this collection is a wall. Two hundred years earlier, someone in Nubia painted a face on the cathedral at Faras; Saint Anne now hangs in the National Museum in Warsaw, lifted off that wall as a thin slab of plaster in the 1960s by a Polish expedition racing the reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam, and shared out under a division of finds agreed with Sudan. Both were made as part of a building, for one place, facing one way; both now stand free in a European room. There the removal was negotiated, recorded and split. Here it took a warship's crew, a sledge and a raft, and the island has asked for the thing back.

replacedBy.beside: Go back to the sockets under that brow: the deepest cuts on the figure, made to hold eyes of white coral that are gone. Saint Anne, painted on the cathedral wall at Faras some two centuries earlier and kept today by Warsaw's National Museum, is an ancestor too, named by her inscription as mother of the God-bearer, and her face follows the same plan: long, narrow, mouth shut, everything spent on the eyes. Hers survive, two great dark-rimmed almonds above a finger pressed to her lips. Both faces were made to keep watch without speaking. The painted grandmother still does; the carved ancestor's watching was an inlay, and without it the strongest carving on the stone is a hole.

beside: Van Dyck's Filippo Cattaneo, painted eighty years later, sets a boy of roughly the same age against the same problem from the opposite side. That child is a Genoese heir, and van Dyck lets him stay a child: soft dress, a small dog, nothing borrowed from the world of grown men. Titian does the reverse. He hangs a twelve-year-old with a knight's cross, a sword, fur and satin, the full apparatus of an adult office conferred before it could be earned. Both painters know the face gives the years away. One protects the boyhood and paints around it; the other stages the collision and lets the strain of it show.

replacedBy.beside: Rank given to a child is also the subject of Van Dyck's Filippo Cattaneo, in the same Washington collection and painted eighty-two years later. That sitter is four and gets a grandee's whole bearing: full length on a stone step, a gold-shot suit, one hand on his hip, the other holding a mastiff on a chain, his eyes straight on ours. Ranuccio, at twelve, is given something more exact: a white eight-pointed cross on the dark cloak, the badge of his order, and a gilt sword hilt at his hip. The stance is what he lacks. Cut off below the hips, with no step to lift him, he turns his eyes aside, wearing a knight's insignia without a knight's bearing.
